planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; Raven holds its near-black color best out of hot afternoon sun.

directions: Raven arose as a seedling of 'Lily Lovell' and carries that parent's reflexed flower shape, but in an unusually dark, nearly jet-black purple with a faint reddish luster and a small white eye. The finely cut green foliage is marked with maroon blotches near the center and makes a dense, weed-suppressing clump even before bloom. Site it in a shaded border or woodland edge where the dark flowers will show against lighter-leaved neighbors, since they can disappear visually in deep shade or against dark mulch. Shear the flowering stems to the basal foliage once bloom fades to tidy the plant and encourage fresh growth through summer.

common_name: Lohfelden Bigroot Geranium (Compact Pale Pink Cranesbill)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring to early fall in any well-drained soil from full sun to full shade; Lohfelden's shorter habit makes it well suited to edging or small-space groundcover where taller macrorrhizum cultivars would sprawl too far.

directions: Introduced by the Klose nursery in Lohfelden, Germany, this is one of the shortest bigroot geranium selections, forming a dense rhizomatous mat of aromatic, lobed leaves that color orange and red in fall. The flowers open very pale pink, almost white, with darker pink veining and contrasting dark pink anthers, a softer effect than the more common magenta-flowered forms of the species. Like other bigroot geraniums it shrugs off dry shade, root competition from trees and shrubs, and poor soil once established, making it a reliable underplanting for shaded foundations or woodland paths. Cut back old foliage in late winter to refresh the clump before new growth emerges.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Plenum Double Himalayan Geranium (Birch's Double Cranesbill)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained garden soil in sun to full shade; because the double flowers set no seed, deadheading is unnecessary and the plant simply reblooms lightly later in the season.

directions: Also sold under the older trade name 'Birch Double' or 'Birch's Double', this sterile sport produces fully double flowers that open violet-blue tinged with lavender and age to a streaked lilac-pink, resembling tiny ruffled rosettes rather than the typical five-petaled cranesbill form. The pale green, deeply cut foliage spreads into a low mat and turns crimson in autumn, giving two seasons of interest from a single planting. It adapts to nearly any garden condition, including dry shade under shrubs, and is useful at the front of a border or cascading over a low wall. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; like the species, Whiteknights resents winter wet and performs best in a rock garden or raised bed where water does not sit at the crown.

directions: Named for the Whiteknights campus garden where it was selected, this cultivar departs from the typical white, purple-veined species flower by opening pale lavender with darker purple veining instead. Its felted, wrinkled, sage-gray leaves are shallowly lobed and nearly as ornamental as the flowers, holding their texture through the growing season in lean, dry soil. Grow it where its low mound can be appreciated up close, such as along a path edge or atop a dry stone wall, since both foliage and bloom are easily hidden by taller, lusher neighbors. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which encourages floppy growth and crown rot over winter.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this white form of wood cranesbill flowers most heavily where it gets reliable moisture through spring and early summer.

directions: Traced back to a collection made in northern Sweden in the 1940s, this is the pure white-flowered form of the European wood cranesbill, bearing well-branched heads of inch-wide blooms held above a crown of knobby rhizomes in late spring. Fresh pale green leaves emerge early and stay tidy through the season, forming a neat clump rather than the sprawling mats typical of many other hardy geraniums. It is happiest in cool, damp woodland conditions and pairs well with ferns, hellebores, and other shade perennials along a border edge or path. Divide in early spring or immediately after flowering if the clump needs rejuvenating.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this dwarf white form is well suited to rock gardens, troughs, and wall crevices where its low mat can spill over an edge.

directions: This white-flowered sport of the dwarf Dalmatian cranesbill forms a tight, mounding mat of glossy, palmately lobed leaves that turn red in fall, smothered in a long summer flush of white blooms touched with the faintest pink. Its diminutive scale and tidy habit suit rock gardens, raised beds, and the front edge of a border, where larger hardy geraniums would quickly overwhelm it. It tolerates both dry, sunny sites and light shade, though sharp drainage is essential. Propagate by division in spring when the mat becomes congested.

common_name: Clos du Coudray Knotted Geranium (Shade Cranesbill)

planting.note: Plant in ordinary garden soil in partial to full shade; it tolerates more sun than most shade geraniums if the soil stays reliably moist, and self-sown seedlings come true to the parent's color.

directions: Discovered as a garden seedling in Normandy, France, this selection of the woodland-tolerant knotted cranesbill bears mauve-violet flowers edged in pale pink and streaked with darker violet veining, set above glossy, embossed dark green leaves adapted to low light. It flowers from spring into early autumn with minimal deadheading and colonizes shaded ground readily by both rhizomes and self-sown seed, making it a dependable filler under trees and shrubs where little else thrives. The foliage often takes on reddish-orange tones in cooler weather, adding interest after the main flush of bloom fades. Thin or transplant volunteer seedlings in spring to control spread.

planting.note: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the trailing stems scramble over nearby plants or a low wall and bloom continuously from early summer to the first frosts with no deadheading required.

directions: A Dutch-bred selection of the Himalayan cranesbill, Havana Blues opens unusually large, saucer-shaped lavender-blue flowers with prominent dark blue veining and a white central zone, carried over a long season on sprawling, trailing stems. Young foliage emerges marbled with light yellow before settling to green, adding a second layer of interest beneath the flowers. Its low, spreading habit makes it useful for underplanting roses and shrubs, tumbling through a mixed border, or filling gaps at the front of a bed, and deer tend to leave it alone. Cut the stems back hard in early summer if growth becomes congested.

common_name: Dirigo Ice Woodland Phlox (Pale Ice-Blue Wild Sweet William)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, non-chalky soil in partial shade to full sun; stems root readily where they touch the ground, so top-dress lightly with compost to encourage the mat to knit together.

directions: Originating in Maine, Dirigo Ice bears fragrant, lilac-white flowers with a faint pale violet eye, a cooler and icier tone than the more common sky-blue woodland phlox selections. The semi-evergreen foliage forms a loose carpet that roots along short, trailing stems, filling in steadily around taller shade perennials without becoming aggressive. It flowers heavily for several weeks in mid-spring and tolerates considerably more sun than most woodland phlox provided the soil stays consistently moist. Shear lightly after bloom to maintain a tidy mound and encourage fresh foliage through summer.

common_name: White Perfume Woodland Phlox (Fragrant White Wild Sweet William)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; siting it near a path or seating area lets its fragrance carry during the spring bloom period.

directions: White Perfume carries loose clusters of fragrant, pure white, saucer-shaped flowers above a low, spreading mat of semi-evergreen foliage in April and May, among the most strongly scented of the white woodland phlox selections. It spreads gently by trailing, rooting stems rather than aggressive runners, making it easy to keep within bounds at the front of a shaded border or along a woodland path. Its clean white flowers show especially well against darker-leaved companions like heuchera or hellebore, and the fragrance is most noticeable on mild, still spring evenings. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Blue Buttons Wild Sweet William (Unnotched Woodland Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; keep soil moisture consistent through establishment, though once rooted this subspecies tolerates drier shade than typical ssp. divaricata.

directions: Phlox divaricata subsp. laphamii is a Midwestern form of woodland phlox distinguished from the typical subspecies by petals that lack the notched tip, and 'Blue Buttons' selects for an especially deep, lavender-blue, fragrant flower color over low mounds of narrow, dark green leaves. Leafy shoots root at the nodes as they spread, letting established plantings form broad, early-spring drifts under deciduous trees and shrubs. It is a reliable pollinator draw in a season when few other shade perennials are blooming, and its drought tolerance once established makes it a forgiving choice for root-filled shade. Divide and replant sections after flowering if the patch needs rejuvenating.

common_name: Wister Pink Creeping Phlox (Soft Pink Woodland Groundcover Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants about a foot apart so the low mat fills in over one to two seasons.

directions: Wister Pink forms an especially low, calmly spreading mat of dark green, rounded leaves only a few inches tall, with large soft pink flowers held just above the foliage on short stems in early spring. It spreads by short rooting runners rather than aggressive stolons, making it easier to keep in bounds than some other creeping phlox selections while still forming a dense carpet over a few seasons. Its compact scale suits small woodland gaps, shaded rock garden pockets, or the front edge of a shaded border where taller groundcovers would overwhelm neighboring plants. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat tidy and divide congested clumps in fall if flowering declines.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society Plant Finder
